patient_information: A 32-year-old Malawian man who is known to be HIV positive. He was started on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis two months prior to presentation. A recent CD4 count was 95 cells/μL. He had a past medical history of treatment for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) sputum smear-negative pulmonary tuberculosis 12 years ago.
chief_complaint: A 6-week history of productive cough, chest pain, and a painfully swollen neck.
history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 6-week history of productive cough and chest pain, associated with weight loss, fevers, and night sweats. During this period, he also noticed a painful swelling in his neck. He reported no other symptoms. His symptoms developed approximately one month after initiating antiretroviral therapy for HIV.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a resident of Malawi. He had not left Malawi, where multi-drug resistance for tuberculosis is reported to be uncommon. No other specific exposures were mentioned.
vitals: On examination, his temperature was 39.2°C (102.56°F), pulse was 112 bpm, and respiratory rate was 28 breaths per minute. His blood pressure was noted to be normal.
physical_exam: The patient appeared moderately ill, pale, and was sweating. The key finding on physical examination was the presence of large, matted lymph glands palpable in his neck. The rest of the examination was unremarkable.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial full blood count showed a WBC of 14.3x10^9/L, hemoglobin of 6.3 g/dL, MCV of 66 fL, and platelets of 246x10^9/L. Three sputum samples were negative for AFB. A fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of a neck gland yielded purulent material that was 2+ positive for AFB on microscopy. A blood culture showed no growth. Follow-up investigations after a lack of clinical improvement revealed an increased CD4 count of 109 cells/μL and an HIV-1 RNA level of <400 copies/mL. A repeat FBC showed WBC 7.8x10^9/L, hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL, MCV 84 fL, and platelets 428x10^9/L. A second FNA of the increasingly fluctuant neck swelling showed frank yellowish pus with numerous coccoid bacteria and polymorphonuclear lymphocytes on microscopy; bacterial culture results were never received.
differential_diagnosis: Given the poor initial response to standard anti-tuberculous treatment, several possibilities were considered. These included infection with atypical mycobacteria, non-adherence to therapy, drug malabsorption, or drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Paradoxical immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) was also a strong consideration. The frank fluctuation of the lymph nodes also raised the probability of a bacterial superinfection, while lymphoma seemed less likely.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was admitted and started on a repeat treatment regimen for tuberculous lymphadenitis, consisting of streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, while continuing his ART. After three weeks, he failed to improve, with persistent fevers, night sweats, and worsening fluctuant swelling of his neck glands. Due to suspicion of paradoxical IRIS, corticosteroids were initiated. A second FNA was performed which suggested a bacterial superinfection. The patient subsequently recovered well after incision and drainage of the neck abscess, antibiotic treatment, and a short course of corticosteroids, while continuing his TB treatment and ART.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was tuberculous lymphadenitis with a superimposed bacterial lymphadenitis, occurring in the context of paradoxical immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). The diagnosis of tuberculosis was established by a fine-needle aspirate from a neck lymph node that was 2+ positive for acid-fast bacilli. The bacterial superinfection, possibly iatrogenic from the initial aspiration, was diagnosed based on a second aspirate showing pus with coccoid bacteria and a dramatic clinical improvement following incision, drainage, and antibiotic therapy. The clinical worsening despite appropriate anti-tuberculous therapy, in the setting of a rising CD4 count after starting ART, was characteristic of IRIS.
